result:
A connection pool keeps a set of already-open database connections alive and lends them out to requests, instead of opening and closing a fresh connection each time. When your code needs the database it borrows an idle connection, runs its queries, and returns it to the pool rather than closing it; if none are idle, the pool either opens a new one (up to a configured maximum) or makes the caller wait until one is returned.

It helps because opening a connection is expensive: a TCP handshake, usually TLS, authentication, and session setup on the server, which in Postgres means forking a whole process. That can cost several milliseconds to tens of milliseconds, often more than the query itself, so reusing connections removes that overhead from every request.

The cap on pool size matters just as much. Each connection consumes memory and scheduling capacity on the database, so a traffic spike with unpooled connections can exhaust the server's connection limit or thrash it. A pool turns that overload into orderly queueing on the application side, which keeps the database at a throughput it can sustain.

The main things to get right are the size (bigger is not better; a small pool, often around a few times the database's core count, usually outperforms a large one) and always returning connections, since a leaked connection is permanently lost capacity and eventually stalls the app when the pool runs dry.
